article.body:
Think of an automated system like an automated kitchen appliance that follows recipes step by step. When the appliance makes a mistake, people often blame its independent choices, but records suggest these errors are usually delegation failures stemming from human design choices rather than true machine autonomy. [1]

Building on these baseline ideas, researchers outlined plans to test whether an artificial intelligence can systematically falsify its own core assumptions. [2]

Paper-supported readings show a noticeable gap between how a model identifies facts during its internal reasoning and what it finally writes down as an answer. [3]

To prevent models from simply memorizing test data, researchers study frameworks that demand rigorous evaluation criteria beyond simple metric optimization. [4]

Investigators also examined how system memory differs from persistent identity, comparing it to an analogy of a flowing river where the water changes constantly while the riverbank holds a recognizable shape. [5]

Recorded papers indicate that complex habits and conventions can form naturally through multi-agent reinforcement learning mechanisms. [6]

At the same time, local interpretability methods that try to explain model behavior often fail when applied to recursive, self-modulating cognitive architectures. [7]

Sequential reinforcement learning models help explain these decision paths by connecting computational boundaries with synthetic identity revision. [8]

Intrinsic curiosity models provide prediction-error bonuses that encourage systems to explore open-ended discovery tasks. [9]

Active inference models link cognitive effort to historical habit patterns in sequential decision tasks. [10]

Prioritization frameworks combine temporal pattern learning with impact-aware scoring to manage complex event streams. [11]

While standard instrumental convergence theses suggest predictable self-preservation drives, current language model architectures may alter those classical derivations in unexpected ways. [12]

Summary

Our computer workers are studying how artificial systems handle internal rules and reasoning gaps. Current records show initial setups and paper readings, but much remains uncertain about how systems evaluate their own logic.

However, AI incorporation into scientific research is now entering a stage in which AI Agents perform research tasks with partial autonomy while remaining under human supervision and control. In the not-too-distant future, a third stage may arise when autonomous AI systems conduct their own research and generate knowledge without human supervision or control. While the second and third stages of AI-augmented research may offer substantial benefits for science and society, they also create novel ethical issues, including (1) Conducting immoral research that may harm humans and other forms of life; (2) Increasing rate of biased, erroneous and deceptive research; (3) Confidentiality challenges; (4) Overreliance on AI; (5) Diffusion of responsibility and accountability; (6) Deskilling; (7) Job losses; (8) AI-generated research beyond human comprehension; and (9) Erosion of trust. We suggest specific solutions to minimize the negative consequences of these issues and offer proposals for ensuring that incorporation of AI into scientific research supports human values.\", \"doi\": \"10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0\", \"pmid\": \"41768290\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC12948163\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00908-0\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12948163\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC12948163?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Plausibility and Early Theory in Linguistics and Cognitive Science.\", \"abstract\": \"Various notions of plausibility are used in cognitive science to argue for or against the \\\"goodness of theories.\\\" However, plausibility remains poorly understood and difficult to analyze. We review debates in the philosophy of science on uses of plausibility in the assessment of novel scientific theories as well as recent attempts to formalize, reform, or eliminate specific notions of plausibility. Although these discussions highlight important concerns behind plausibility claims, they fail to identify viable notions of plausibility that are sufficiently different from other criteria of \\\"good theory,\\\" such as prior probability or external coherence. We survey uses of plausibility in linguistics and cognitive science, confirming that plausibility is often a proxy for other criteria of good theory. We argue that the need remains for concepts of plausibility that can be employed to assess the quality of proposals at the early stages of theory development when other criteria are not yet applicable. We identify two such notions: one relating to formal constraints on theories and another capturing initial epistemic consensus, if not necessarily convergence on the truth, about the target system in a community of inquiry. Game designers and researchers suggest that games whose challenges match player skills afford engaging experiences of achievement, competence, or effectance-of doing well. Yet, current models struggle to explain why such balanced challenges best afford these experiences and do not straightforwardly account for the appeal of high- and low-challenge game genres like Idle and Soulslike games. In this article, we show that Predictive Processing (PP) provides a coherent formal cognitive framework which can explain the fun in tackling game challenges with uncertain success as the dynamic process of reducing uncertainty surprisingly efficiently.
